title: The happiest country in the world

fn.en: Talk about happiness factors; talk about the result of a real condition.

gr: the real (first) conditional, with if, unless, as long as and provided that

can.en: I can say what will happen if a real condition is met — and what will not, unless it is.

sub.en: These are real possibilities. Look at the tense in each half.

items.q: If people ___ a thirty-seven-hour week, they have real leisure time.
items.why: The if clause takes a present tense, even though it is about the future.

items.q: If you cycle for half an hour a day, it ___ add a year or two to your life.
items.why: The result clause can take will, may, might, can or an imperative — not only will.

items.q: ___ everybody has enough, money does not make a country happy.
items.why: unless = if … not. Never say “unless … not”.

items.q: ___ a society is reasonably equal, the system seems to work.
You will be healthier ___ you spend some time outdoors every day.
If you ___ a decision early in the day, you ___ probably make a better one.
If you have too much information, you ___ more likely to choose wrongly.
items.why: When both halves are always true, the present simple appears twice.

items.q: ___ you tired today, or is it the weather?
items.why: RECYCLED from Lesson 20: with be, no auxiliary is added.

unless already means if … not, so a second negative is wrong.
This is a real possibility, so the first conditional is used.

acts.title: The happiest country in the world
text: Every year a report ranks the countries of the world by how content their people say they are, and every year the same small northern countries sit at the top. Denmark is usually one of them. The interesting question is not why the Danes are happy, but what, if anything, the rest of us can take from it. The same three factors come up.

The first is money, but not in the way people assume. Denmark has a strong economy and very little poverty. The cost of living is high, but so are wages. However, if you look further down the list, you find Mexico above the United States. Money does not make a country happy unless everybody has enough of it. Big differences between rich and poor tend to make everybody less content, including the rich.

The second is what the money is spent on. If a country collects high taxes, as Denmark does, it can provide healthcare and childcare to everyone. You may not believe that you will be happier if you pay more tax, but as a society you will.

The third is time. The Danes work about thirty-seven hours a week. If people work a thirty-seven-hour week, they have real leisure time, and they spend a good deal of it on cultural activities and on seeing other people. They tend to eat a balanced diet, too. Half of all journeys to work and school in Copenhagen are made by bicycle, and doctors estimate that if you cycle for half an hour a day, you may add a year or two to your life.

None of this is a secret, and none of it needs a Danish passport. As long as a society is reasonably equal, provides for everybody and leaves people time, it seems to work. Unless those three things are true, very little else does.

items.s: According to the text, money alone is enough to make a country happy.
Mexico appears higher on the list than the United States.
High taxes allow Denmark to provide healthcare to everybody.
The Danes work an average of about fifty hours a week.
Half of all journeys to work and school in Copenhagen are made by bicycle.
The writer says only Denmark could ever achieve this.

items.sit: You are giving somebody practical advice about a real possibility.
o: If you cycle to work, you’ll sleep better.
If you will cycle to work, you’ll sleep better.
If you would cycle to work, you’d sleep better.

items.sit: You want to say that something is only true when a condition is not met.
o: Unless you have close friends, it’s hard to be content.
Unless you don’t have close friends, it’s hard to be content.
If not you have close friends, it’s hard to be content.

items.sit: You are naming the one condition on which you agree.
o: As long as everybody gets a turn, I don’t mind.
As long as everybody will get a turn, I don’t mind.

items.sit: You want to leave the result less certain than “will”.
o: If you go outside every day, you may feel better.
If you go outside every day, you will may feel better.
If you will go outside every day, you may feel better.

items.sit: You are stating something that is always true.

If you will have too much information, you choose badly.
If you would have too much information, you choose badly.

write.q: Write about what would actually make your city or your workplace a better place to be. Use the real conditional at least four times, and include one unless and one as long as or provided that.
plan: something that will not work unless…
write.model: If the city finishes the bus lane on Bukhar Zhyrau, about half the people I know will stop driving to work. That sounds small, but if forty thousand people stop driving, the air in February changes. It will not work unless the buses actually run every six minutes — nobody gives up a car for a bus they cannot rely on. I would support paying for it through higher parking charges, provided that the money goes back into the network rather than into the general budget. As long as people can see where the money went, they will accept almost anything. If nothing changes, we will simply have the same argument again in five years.

speak.q: Talk for about a minute: what would make people where you live more content? Say what will happen if the change is made, and what will not happen unless a second condition is met.
speak.model: If the city finishes the bus lane, half the people I know will stop driving. But it won’t work unless the buses run every six minutes — nobody gives up a car for a bus they can’t rely on. I’d pay for it through parking charges, provided that the money goes back into the network. As long as people see where the money went, they’ll accept it.
